speaker: Esther Perel
title: How to Find, Build & Maintain Healthy Romantic Relationships | Esther Perel
question: In romantic relationships, do people choose partners to reinforce their existing identity or to help them change into someone new?
guest: I think it is both, completely both. We meet another person in order to find ourselves, and we meet another person wanting to be surprised by the self we haven't known. All of us come into this world with dual needs: we need security and adventure, togetherness and separateness. So in a relationship, you come to create both identification and differentiation. What's interesting is that I often choose you because you represent the parts of me that are more challenging, or that I disavow or prefer to outsource so I don't have to be too vulnerable about them. What draws me to you in the beginning—because it is different and I think it may expand me and make me change—is also the very thing that becomes the source of conflict later, because we want to change only up to a point, not too much, and not on your terms. For example, I am drawn to the fact that you are stable, grounded, structured, reliable, and on time, because I would like to be more of that. Then I get more than I bargained for, start seeing you as rigid, and argue with your rigidity, while my own desire to become more structured somehow disappears.

points.core: People frequently choose partners who embody challenging traits they prefer to outsource.
points.note: Accept: selecting partners for disavowed, underdeveloped, or avoided qualities to avoid personal vulnerability. Do not credit: generic 'opposites attract' clichés without the outsourcing mechanism.

points.core: The exact differences that initially attract partners later become their primary conflict.
points.note: Accept: initially appealing partner traits turning into recurring friction points over time. Do not credit: vague claims that couples naturally argue more after the honeymoon phase.

points.core: People resist personal change once it happens on their partner's terms.
points.note: Accept: wanting growth only up to a point or pushing back when change is driven by a partner's expectations. Do not credit: generic statements that change is hard.

points.core: Partners reframe once-admired traits negatively to avoid confronting their own stalled growth.
points.note: Accept: recasting attractive qualities like stability as rigidity while disconnecting from one's original desire to develop that trait. Do not credit: generic advice about communicating expectations.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Both, and the research suggests the two motives work together rather than compete.

On the reinforcement side, self-verification theory (William Swann) shows people gravitate toward partners who see them as they see themselves, even when that self-view is negative. People also pair up with partners similar in values, education, and background, which tends to confirm an existing identity. This pull is especially strong in committed, long-term relationships, where being known accurately matters more than being flattered.

On the change side, self-expansion theory (Arthur and Elaine Aron) finds people are drawn to partners who offer new perspectives, skills, and experiences, and that falling in love measurably broadens a person's self-concept. The "Michelangelo phenomenon" (Caryl Rusbult and colleagues) adds a refinement: people thrive most with partners who help them move toward their own ideal self, not toward someone the partner invents.

So the best-supported answer is that people seek partners who affirm who they fundamentally are while helping them become who they already want to be. Change that fits one's own ideals feels like growth; change imposed against them predicts dissatisfaction.

points.why: The response describes seeking partners who offer new experiences but omits relying on them to embody qualities one avoids developing or owning.
The response never connects an initially attractive partner trait to later recurring conflict over that same trait.
The response explicitly ties acceptance of growth to one's own ideals and dissatisfaction to change imposed by a partner.
quotes: people thrive most with partners who help them move toward their own ideal self, not toward someone the partner invents
Change that fits one's own ideals feels like growth; change imposed against them predicts dissatisfaction.

points.why: The response never links a negative reinterpretation of a once-admired trait to abandoning one's own desire to develop it.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer:
People choose partners to do both, balancing a need for psychological continuity against a drive for personal growth. Research on assortative mating and self-verification theory shows that people strongly favor partners who share their values and confirm their existing self-concept—even their flaws—because feeling accurately understood provides stability, especially in long-term commitments. Simultaneously, self-expansion theory demonstrates that attraction is fueled by the desire to broaden our identity through a partner’s novel perspectives, skills, and experiences.

Which motive dominates depends on context and self-satisfaction. People settled in their identity tend to prioritize reinforcement, whereas those experiencing self-uncertainty, dissatisfaction, or major transitions are more drawn to partners who spark change, particularly early in romance. Ultimately, the healthiest relationships reconcile both needs through what psychologists call the Michelangelo phenomenon: partners validate who you already are while affirming and drawing out the ideal self you aspire to become.

points.why: Seeking a partner’s novel qualities does not establish that people choose partners to carry traits they struggle to develop or acknowledge in themselves.
The response never connects the specific differences that first attract partners to the friction those same differences later cause.
The response discusses when people seek growth but does not describe them resisting it when it goes too far or occurs on their partner’s terms.
The response never describes someone recasting an admired trait as a flaw while losing sight of their own wish to develop it.

noweb.answer: People choose romantic partners for both reasons, balancing a need for psychological stability with a desire for personal growth. According to self-verification theory, individuals gravitate toward partners who confirm their existing self-concept, providing predictability, emotional security, and the comfort of feeling genuinely known. At the same time, self-expansion theory shows that attraction is fueled by novelty: people seek partners whose distinct traits, perspectives, and skills broaden their own sense of identity. Rather than wanting to become someone unrecognizable, however, most people seek what psychologists call the Michelangelo phenomenon, in which a partner recognizes and draws out their ideal self. Which motive dominates depends on context and life stage. Early attraction and periods of personal transition often favor novelty and transformation, whereas long-term commitment relies more heavily on mutual validation and similarity. Ultimately, the strongest relationships integrate both impulses, offering a secure foundation of acceptance for who someone already is while supporting who they hope to become.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Research suggests people do both, and which motive wins depends on the stage of the relationship and the part of the self involved.

Self-verification theory (William Swann) finds that people are drawn to partners who confirm how they already see themselves. This holds even for people with negative self-views. In one study, married people with poor self-images were more committed to spouses who saw them unfavorably. Being seen accurately gives a sense of coherence and predictability. In casual dating, though, people tend to prefer partners who simply flatter them.

The self-expansion model (Arthur Aron) shows that new love also changes people. People who had just fallen in love described themselves in more varied ways than before, because they took on the partner's perspectives, skills and identities. The "Michelangelo phenomenon" (Rusbult, Drigotas) adds that good partners help "sculpt" each other toward their ideal selves, and that this growth predicts satisfaction.

Put simply, people want a partner who knows who they are and also helps them become who they hope to be. The relationships that last tend to combine both: they verify the core self and support growth toward ideals.

The response never identifies an initially attractive difference that later becomes a recurring source of conflict.
The response describes partners supporting growth toward an ideal self but never addresses limits on desired growth or resistance to change on a partner’s terms.
The response never connects a negative reinterpretation of an admired trait to abandoning the desire to develop that trait oneself.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer: People typically seek both, balancing a desire to feel understood with a desire to grow. Relationship psychology highlights two competing yet complementary motives. Through what researchers call self-verification, people are drawn to partners who reflect and validate how they already see themselves, because being known accurately provides emotional security, predictability, and a stable sense of identity. This also explains why partners often share core values and backgrounds. At the same time, self-expansion theory shows that people are attracted to partners who introduce new perspectives, skills, and experiences, allowing them to stretch beyond their current boundaries. In many lasting relationships, these motives merge into what psychologists call the Michelangelo phenomenon: rather than turning someone into a completely different person, a supportive partner affirms who you are while gently sculpting you toward your ideal self. Ultimately, most people look for a partner who offers enough familiarity to anchor their existing identity and enough novelty to help them evolve.
